declarations.name: anchorElement
declarations.description:
The element a floating surface should open against, given the slot it wraps.

**A wrapper with no box is not an anchor.** `display: contents` puts an
element's children into the layout and leaves the element itself without a
box, so its `getBoundingClientRect()` is `0 0 0 0`. Measured: a tooltip host
reports exactly that while the button inside it reports 32 by 32. Anchoring
to it opens the surface against the top left of the window, and focusing it
on close puts focus nowhere.

That is not an edge case, because wrapping is how a tooltip attaches to the
thing it describes. Without this, an icon button used as a trigger is the one
button on a toolbar that cannot have a tooltip.

So this descends past anything that draws nothing, and the first child with a
box is the anchor. The wrapper is transparent by construction, so the thing
with the box is the thing the reader is pointing at.

Bounded rather than a walk to the leaves: a chain of box-less wrappers is
already unusual, and descending without a limit through a tree this library
does not own is worse than stopping and anchoring to something imperfect.

declarations.name: capturePointer
declarations.description:
Takes the pointer for a drag, and carries on if the platform refuses.

**Capture is an enhancement, and the drag has to survive losing it.** What it
buys is events continuing to arrive once the pointer leaves the target, which
matters because a thin divider is easy to outrun. What it costs, called bare,
is the rest of the handler: `setPointerCapture` throws `NotFoundError` when
the id names no active pointer, and every one of these calls sits above the
lines that set the dragging flag and call `preventDefault`. So a refusal did
not degrade the drag, it cancelled it.

That is reachable outside a test: a pointer released between the event being
queued and the handler running is gone by the time this is called, and a
synthetic `pointerdown` has no active pointer at all. The browser spec run
reported four of those as uncaught page errors, and three splitter specs had
each stubbed the method to get past it, which is the shape of a workaround
that has been in place long enough to read as setup.

Returns whether it took, for the callers that then ask `hasPointerCapture`
before believing a move belongs to them.

declarations.name: closestInstance
declarations.description:
The nearest ancestor that is an instance of a class, crossing shadow roots.

**Identity rather than tag name, and the rule already existed.** `Accordion`'s
root states it two files from a violation of it: "Items are matched with
`instanceof`, never by tag name. Matching `helix-accordion-item` would tie
this tier to the styled one." Nine headless families resolve their
relationships that way; two did it by tag, and both named `helix-*` tags that
only `@helix-io/web` registers, which is a headless package depending on a
styled one by string.

The consequence is silent rather than loud. Subclassing a base element under
a different tag is exactly what the headless tier exists to allow, and it is
what `helix/web` itself does. Under a third tag the lookup returned `null`,
so an accordion's `mode` was ignored and every section behaved as `multiple`
with no error anywhere.

**`closest()` alone is not enough**, which is why this walks rather than
delegating. `closest()` stops at a shadow boundary: a component slotted into
another component's shadow root has a `parentNode` chain that ends at a
`ShadowRoot`, and `closest` will not step across it. Following `host` is what
makes a nested arrangement resolve, and nesting through a slot is the
ordinary case for anything composable.

declarations.name: createSheet
declarations.description:
Builds a stylesheet from CSS authored in a `.css` file.

Component styles live in real `.css` files rather than `css` tagged
templates, so they get CSS tooling: syntax highlighting, formatters, the
token linter, and a diff that reads as CSS. `bun run styles` compiles each
one into a sibling `.css.ts` that calls this.

The `unsafe` in `unsafeCSS` warns about interpolating untrusted input into a
stylesheet. That is not what happens here: the argument is a build-time
constant read from a file in this repo, never a runtime value. Wrapping it
keeps the warning where it belongs, on `unsafeCSS` itself, and gives one seam
to change if constructable stylesheets become the better primitive.

declarations.name: customElement
declarations.description:
Registers a custom element, once.

A drop-in replacement for Lit's `@customElement` that does not throw when the
tag is already registered.

The duplicate is not hypothetical. Next.js evaluates a module in both the
server and client graphs, so a component imported by a server component and a
client component runs its registration twice against one registry, and
`customElements.define` throws:

> Failed to execute 'define': the name "helix-card" has already been used

That failure takes down the whole prerender, and it appears only once an app
mixes server and client usage of the same component, which is exactly what a
real app does.

The analyzer detects `@customElement` **by decorator name**, not by where it
is imported from, so the manifest still records `tagName` and nothing
downstream changes.

declarations.name: drawIcon
declarations.description:
Draws an icon that was imported by name, rather than looked up by string.

**`<helix-icon name="play">` indexes the whole icon set at runtime.** Its
render is `icons[this.name]`, and no bundler can shake a dynamic index, so
every consumer of any component that renders one ships all of the generated
path data: measured at 50,814 bytes raw and 15,010 gzipped for 102 icons, and
growing about 147 gzipped bytes per icon added. A named import ships one path
and is checked when the package compiles rather than when `check:icons` runs.

That element still earns its place as *public* API, where a consumer writes a
name in markup and a lookup is the only thing that can work. What it should
not be is how this library draws its own marks.

**There is no `part` option, and there cannot be.** A part name behind an
interpolation is a part the manifest cannot see, so `check:selectors` reports
the component's own stylesheet as matching nothing and the part stops being
API. `Trend` needs one and therefore writes its `<svg>` out with a literal
`part="icon"`, which is the honest cost: a helper can carry everything except
the thing static analysis has to read.

`data-glyph` rather than a class, because the sizing lives in
`helix/web/src/icon/glyph.css` and a component's own `--icon-size`
declarations have to keep working untouched: the variable was read by
`helix-icon`, and now it is read by the rule that sheet carries. Without it
every one of those declarations would go quietly dead and every mark in six
families would change size.

declarations.name: drawTooltip
declarations.description:
What a pointer resting on a reading shows, as `Tooltip` pointed at a mark.

**A chart does not draw its own tooltip, and the top layer is why.** `Tooltip`
renders `popover="manual"` through `PopoverController`, so it clears every
stacking context and every `overflow` on the page. A box drawn by the chart is
`position: absolute` inside the plot and is confined to the chart's own
context, so it is clipped by, or layered under, whatever sits beside the
chart. Escaping that means reimplementing `PopoverController`, which is
`Tooltip` with extra steps and a second copy of the hard part.

**`for` was already the anchor and needed nothing added.** It resolves through
`getRootNode().getElementById()`, and a chart's shadow root *is* a
`ShadowRoot`, so a chart names an element inside itself and `Tooltip` finds
it. What the chart provides is an invisible mark at the reading's point.

**An HTML mark rather than the `<rect>` or `<circle>` already there.**
`FloatingController` types its anchor as `HTMLElement` and an SVG element is
not one; and a slice's `<circle>` has the bounding box of the whole ring
rather than of its arc, so anchoring to it would point at the ring's centre
for every slice.

**And the arrow now follows from placement rather than from a compass.** The
chart says which side it prefers and `FloatingController` moves it if that
side does not fit, which is how a slice at any bearing gets a bubble that
points at it. Four hard-coded sides could not express a bearing, which is what
made the donut's arrow miss its own ring.

**It shows the table's text and not the chart's numbers.** `$128k` is what the
cell says and `128000` is what the drawing measured. Every cell of the row is
here, including columns nothing was plotted from, because a note beside the
figures is most of the reason to want a tooltip.

**Hidden from assistive technology, on purpose.** The table is the accessible
representation and the drawing is `aria-hidden`; a reader on a keyboard gets
the table, which they can reach, rather than a tooltip which they cannot.

declarations.name: focusableElements
declarations.description:
Everything inside `root` the reader can reach with Tab, in document order.

Separate from the focus trap because finding is the half most callers want:
roving tabindex, arrow-key navigation and "focus the first thing" all need
this list and none of them traps anything.

Visibility is tested with `getClientRects()` rather than `offsetParent`,
which is null for anything inside a `position: fixed` container. A drawer is
exactly that, so the `offsetParent` test excluded every control in the thing
being trapped.

declarations.name: deepActiveElement
declarations.description:
The truly focused element, following shadow roots down.

`document.activeElement` stops at the outermost host, so a button inside two
shadow roots reports as the component rather than as itself.

declarations.name: deepContains
declarations.description:
Whether `node` sits inside `root`, following shadow boundaries upward.

`Node.contains` walks `parentNode` and a shadow root's `parentNode` is null,
so it answers false for anything inside a component. Paired with
`deepActiveElement`, which returns exactly such a node, that pairing is a trap
of its own: the two look like they belong together and one of them crosses.

`FocusTrapController` had precisely that, `contains(deepActiveElement())`,
and it is why every dialog and drawer in the library leaked. Focus on a
`helix-button` reports as the `<button>` in its shadow root, which is in no
light-DOM container anywhere, so the trap read every reader as already
outside it.

`host` is reached without naming `ShadowRoot`, which the server has no global
for. This runs from a keydown handler and would never execute there, but a
bare reference is the kind that surfaces as a crash in Lit's result collector
the first time something calls it early.

declarations.name: hostAria
declarations.description:
Writes a host's semantics onto its `ElementInternals`.

Onto internals rather than onto the host, which is the whole point: an
attribute written at upgrade is markup a React consumer's server output never
had, and hydration reports the difference. Internals carry the same meaning
to the accessibility tree and leave the element as the consumer wrote it.

**Empty means absent, and that is the trap this exists for.** Assigning `''`
to `ariaLabel` is not the same as not naming the element: it is a name of no
characters, which a screen reader announces as an unnamed control while every
check for "is it labelled" passes. Every caller had written
`this.label === '' ? null : this.label` and one of them would eventually not.

**Element references are feature-tested rather than assumed.** They are the
only way a host in the light DOM can point at a node in its own shadow root,
an IDREF cannot cross that boundary, and the plain `element.aria*Elements`
reflection drops the reference where `ElementInternals` keeps it. Older
engines have neither, and assigning to a property they do not implement is a
silent no-op rather than an error, so the guard is what makes the absence
visible to anything reading this.

Omitted keys are left alone, so a component that sets its role once in
`willUpdate` and its references later in `updated` does not have to repeat
itself or risk clearing what the other call wrote.

declarations.name: inheritDisabled
declarations.description:
Disables a group's members without forgetting what they said themselves.

A group and its members are two sources for one fact: a member is out of play
if either says so. Written the obvious way that is
`item.disabled = group || item.disabled`, and it latches. The first pass with
the group disabled writes `true` onto every member; the next pass reads its
own writing back as the member's own answer; and enabling the group leaves
every member disabled for good. Nothing about it is visible until something
re-enables a group, which is rare enough to ship and miserable to find.

So what a member said itself is recorded before it is first overridden, and
given back when the group lets go. Restoring is the half that matters: a
version that only recorded would read the overridden value as the member's
own the moment the group was enabled, which is the same latch by a longer
route.

Once given back, the record is dropped, so a consumer disabling a member
afterwards is its own answer again and is left alone.

declarations.name: forgetDisabled
declarations.description:
Forgets what a group recorded about an item.

For an item leaving a group, which would otherwise carry the group's last
word into wherever it goes next.

declarations.name: linePath
declarations.description:
Builds an SVG path through a set of points.

Shared by every chart that draws a line, so the choice of curve is one
implementation rather than one per chart. Pure: it takes points and returns a
string, and knows nothing about elements or lifecycles.

`straight` joins the readings and claims nothing between them, which is why
it is the default. `smooth` is easier to follow across a long series and
invents the values in between, so it is a reading aid rather than a neutral
one. `step` claims the opposite, that a reading holds until the next one, and
changes at the midpoint rather than at either end, since a chart's x axis is
an order and neither neighbour has a better claim on the moment it moved.

Fewer than two points is an empty string rather than a partial path: one
reading is not a line, and `M0,0` alone draws nothing while still being a
path element that looks like it should.

declarations.name: onUnlessFalse
declarations.default: { fromAttribute: (value: string | null): boolean => value !== null && value !== 'false', /* Written out so it survives being reflected later. `''` rather than `'true'`, which is what a boolean attribute looks like everywhere else. */ toAttribute: (value: boolean): string | null => (value ? '' : 'false'), }
declarations.description:
For a boolean property that is on unless a consumer says otherwise.

**Lit's boolean converter cannot express false, and that is the whole
problem.** It answers `value !== null`, so an attribute is true by being
there: `modal` is true, `modal=""` is true, and `modal="false"` is true as
well, because it is present. A property defaulting to `true` therefore has no
attribute that turns it off at all, and a consumer who writes the obvious
thing gets the opposite of what they asked for, silently.

Found on `Drawer.modal`, where it mattered: a tour cannot point inside a
modal, so `modal="false"` is exactly what a consumer reaches for, and it left
the drawer modal. Two others have the same shape, `Video.playsInline` and the
sandbox source's `tabIndents`.

So: absent is the default, present is on, and the one string that means off
is the one a consumer would write. `"false"` only, and not `"0"` or `"no"`,
because a converter that accepts a vocabulary invites a consumer to guess at
it, and the one they guess wrong is the one that silently means on.

**The other answer is to invert the property, and it is worse.** `Drawer`
would take `modeless`, absent meaning modal, which satisfies the rule that a
reflected property takes no default. It also renames the thing every consumer
already writes, to a word nobody reaches for, so that markup can express a
state that is rare. The name stays and the attribute learns to say no.

declarations.name: readRows
declarations.description:
Reads a table as rows rather than as columns.

**Everything `readSeries` throws away on purpose, a tooltip needs.** That
function answers "what should I draw", so it keeps the parsed number and
discards the cell's text, and it drops a column whose cells are not numbers
at all. A chart drawing `128000` and a tooltip saying `128000` would be the
chart overruling the table, which already decided that number reads `$128k`;
and a column of notes beside the figures is exactly the extra a reader wants
when their pointer is resting on a reading.

So this keeps both, and keeps the columns nothing plotted. A chart of two
series over a table of four columns still has four columns to show.

The traversal is the same shape as `readSeries` and deliberately separate.
Folding them into one pass returning both would make every caller who wants
one build the other, and the two are asked for at different moments: series
on render, rows only where a pointer has stopped.

declarations.name: requestControlledChange

parameters.name:
{
  apply,
  controlled,
  event,
  host,
  label,
  next,
  read,
}

declarations.description:
Announces a change, then applies it if nobody refused.

One audited path for every stateful change in the system. The order is the
whole point: the event goes first and carries the state being *proposed*, so
a listener calling `preventDefault()` stops it before anything moves. A
component that mutated itself and then announced it would leave a consumer
reacting to a decision already made.

Returns whether the change was applied, so a caller that needs to know
(a key handler deciding whether to also move focus) can ask.

**There is one channel, and it is the event.** `onCheckedChange`,
`onOpenChange`, `onValueChange` and `onActiveChange` were a second one,
invoked from here once the state had been applied. They were removed on
19 Aug 2026, for working in fewer places than the thing they duplicated:
React takes any `on[A-Z]` prop into its own branch and calls
`addEventListener('CheckedChange', …)` with it, an event nothing dispatches,
so no consumer writing JSX could reach one. The justification written beside
them was that the generated React wrapper assigned them instead, and that
package was deleted in `6bc8502`, which left four documented properties that
only a consumer holding a reference could use. `helix-change` reaches every
consumer in every framework, hydration included.

declarations.name: resolveActiveItem
declarations.description:
Which item a value names, or the first that could stand in for it.

`items.find(match) ?? items[0]` was written by hand in four components and it
is not the obvious line it looks like. It is what makes a set whose `value`
names nothing still show something, which is every set before its consumer
has chosen and every set whose current item has just been removed.

The fallback skips disabled items and the match does not. A consumer who
names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to another would be the
component overruling them; but falling back *onto* a disabled item is the
component choosing, and it should not choose something out of play. Every
hand-written copy took `items[0]` either way, so a set opening on a disabled
first item showed it as current.

A plain function rather than only a method on `MixinControllerActive`,
because the components that need it are split across two mixins: a set whose
value is submitted takes `MixinControllerValue` and cannot also take the
active one without two properties called `value`.

declarations.name: holdCaret
declarations.description:
Holds the caret across a write the element does not make itself.

**Lit's `.value` binding moves the caret to the end, and only a controlled
field notices.** Measured in Chrome with real typing: place the caret after
`Ada` in `Ada Lovelace` and press one key, and an uncontrolled field reports
`AdaX Lovelace` with the caret at 4, while a controlled one reports the same
text with the caret at 13. Editing the middle of a controlled field was
impossible: every keystroke threw the caret to the end.

The asymmetry is the interesting part. Uncontrolled, `handleInput` runs
`restoreValue` after the state has moved, so the control already holds the
new text and the call returns early; when Lit's binding then assigns the same
string, Chrome leaves the selection alone. Controlled, the control has been
put *back* to the old text while the consumer decides, so Lit assigns a
genuinely different string and the platform resets the selection, as it does
for any assignment to `value`.

So the selection is taken before the update and put back after it, mapped by
however much the text grew or shrank, which is the same arithmetic
`restoreValue` does in one step. Returned as a closure rather than a pair of
fields so the two halves cannot be called out of order.

The binding itself has to stay: it is what Lit SSR serializes, and a field
that filled in at hydration would flash empty for every reader on a slow
connection.

declarations.name: extent
declarations.description: The smallest and largest of a set of numbers, as a scale's domain.

declarations.name: linear
declarations.description:
Maps a domain onto a range, linearly.

A pure function rather than a controller, which is the distinction the rules
draw: a controller reacts to a host's lifecycle, and this is arithmetic on
four numbers. It holds nothing, subscribes to nothing, and can be called from
`render` without anything being wired up first.

The range is given rather than assumed, so an inverted one is ordinary: SVG
counts down from the top, so a chart passes `[height, 0]` and gets a larger
value drawn higher without anything here knowing why.

**A flat domain maps to the middle of the range, and that is the case worth
naming.** Every value being equal makes the domain zero wide, and the obvious
arithmetic divides by it: seven identical readings drew a line at `NaN`, which
an `<svg>` renders as no line at all rather than as an error. A flat series is
a real thing to plot and it should come out as a flat line halfway up.

declarations.name: ticks
declarations.description:
The round numbers a reader would infer inside a domain.

**A gridline at an arbitrary number is worse than no gridline.** The point of
a rule across a chart is that a reader can name the level it sits at without
being told, so it has to land on a number a person would have picked: 0, 250,
500, not 187.4. Dividing the domain into equal parts gives the second, and
that is what makes this arithmetic rather than a loop.

The step is the power of ten below the rough interval, multiplied by whichever
of 1, 2, 5 or 10 lands nearest the count asked for. Those four because they
are the multipliers that keep every tick short in decimal, which is the whole
property being bought: 2.5 divides as evenly as 2 and reads as a worse number.

**The count is a target and not a promise**, which is the usual surprise.
Asking for five over a domain of 0 to 1000 gives six (0, 200, ... 1000);
asking for five over 0 to 12 gives seven at a step of 2. Forcing the count
would mean forcing the step, which is the thing worth keeping round. A caller
that needs an exact number of rules wants equal division and not this.

Ticks outside the domain are dropped rather than clamped, so nothing is drawn
off the end of the box and no two rules land on the same line.

A pure function, for the reason `linear` gives beside it: it holds nothing,
subscribes to nothing, and can be called from `render`.

declarations.name: slotFilled
declarations.description:
Whether a consumer put anything in a slot.

**There is no selector for this**, which is why it is script. `slot:empty`
looks like the answer and is not: a slot's children are its *fallback*, and
assigned nodes are not children, so `:empty` is true whenever the fallback is
absent whether or not the consumer slotted anything. `:host(:has(...))` is
invalid CSS, and the server has no children to inspect.

The answer matters because an empty wrapper is not free. A region that
generates a box is a flex item or a grid item whether or not it holds
anything, so it takes the container's gap: an announcement with no actions
paid the row gap twice, a switch with no label took one for a label that was
not there, and a blockquote with no attribution reserved a full space below
every quote. `display: none` is the only fix, because only a box that is not
generated has no gap beside it.

Text or an element, because neither alone is the test. An element on its own
counts a whitespace-only span as content; text on its own counts an icon as
nothing.

`flatten` is deliberate here, unlike the tooltip's emptiness test: this asks
"will anything render", where that one asks "did the consumer provide
anything", and a slot showing its fallback does render.

declarations.name: TONE_MARKS
declarations.default: { danger: { icon: xCircleFill, label: 'Error' }, info: { icon: infoFill, label: 'Information' }, success: { icon: checkCircleFill, label: 'Success' }, warning: { icon: warningFill, label: 'Warning' }, }
declarations.description:
The one status vocabulary.

It was two, defined identically in `Callout` and in `Toast.Item`, and only one
of the copies carried the comment saying the two must not drift. A reader
meets these marks in a passage and in a message and has to read them as the
same four things, so there is one place they come from.

**Filled at every tone**, which is what it already was at one of them.
`danger` took `xCircleFill` and the other three took outlines, so a set meant
to be read as one vocabulary had one member drawn a different way. Filled
because a tone mark is a status indicator and not an action: it wants to
read at a glance and at a small size, where an outline at this weight loses
its interior.

**The label is not the tone name.** `danger` is announced as "Error",
because that is the word a reader understands and `danger` is the word the API
uses. Both matter and they are not the same string.

declarations.name: toneMark
declarations.description:
The mark for a tone, or `undefined` where the name is not one of the four.

A lookup rather than direct indexing, because `tone` reaches a component as an
attribute and an attribute can say anything, including the three tones that
have no mark. Callers decide what an unknown one means: `Callout` falls back
to `info`, since a callout is always *about* something, and `Toast.Item` draws
nothing, since a message is just the next thing that happened.
